result: The authors conducted a scoping review using established frameworks (Arksey and O'Malley, 2005; Levac et al., 2010) to identify reproducibility studies published in 2018-2019 across five disciplines. The search identified 16,135 records from databases plus 159 from grey literature, which after deduplication yielded 11,224 documents for screening, ultimately including 47 documents.
evaluation: Claims C21-C33 describe the methodological approach and search results with specific numbers and procedures. The methodology follows established scoping review frameworks, uses appropriate reporting guidelines (PRISMA-ScR), and provides transparent documentation via OSF. The search strategy was developed by trained specialists and peer-reviewed, supporting the rigor of the approach.

result: The 47 included documents described 177 reproducibility studies total. Most documents (76.6%) described single reproducibility studies, were published in 2018 (59.6%), had corresponding authors from the USA (57.4%), reported funding (68.1% primarily from government sources), and had a median of 3 authors (range 1-172).
evaluation: Claims C34-C48 present descriptive statistics about the included documents. These are straightforward data summaries from the extraction process with specific percentages and counts. The wide range in author numbers (1-172) reflects the inclusion of both individual and large collaborative reproducibility projects, which is reasonable given the study scope.

result: Most reproducibility studies were in psychology (86, 48.6%) and health sciences (42, 23.7%), with smaller numbers in economics (5, 2.8%), education (5, 2.8%), and biomedicine (6, 3.4%). The most common study designs were observational (85, 48.0%) and experimental (52, 29.4%), followed by data re-analysis (35, 19.8%).
evaluation: Claims C49-C58 provide disciplinary and methodological breakdowns of the 177 studies. The data are internally consistent and sum appropriately. The dominance of psychology and health sciences is acknowledged by the authors as potentially reflecting disciplinary cultures around reproducibility, though they appropriately note limitations in generalizability.

result: Most reproducibility studies (66.1%) had no authorship overlap or contact with original study teams. Less than half (45.8%) referred to registered protocols, and only 23.2% used protocols identical to the original study. Data sharing was reported for 63.3% of studies but only 27.7% of documents. Most studies (75.7%) did not report a primary outcome.
evaluation: Claims C59-C67 describe methodological characteristics of the reproducibility studies. The apparent contradiction between study-level (63.3%) and document-level (27.7%) data sharing is explained by the authors—a few multi-study documents drove the higher study-level rate. The lack of primary outcome reporting (75.7%) is concerning and appropriately noted as a limitation.

result: Based on authors' definitions, 53.7% (95/177) of studies reproduced successfully, 20.3% failed, 4.5% had mixed results, and 21.5% could not be assessed. Reproducibility rates varied by discipline: health sciences (85.7%), economics (80%), interdisciplinary (72.7%), biomedicine (66.7%), education (40%), and psychology (29.1%, improving to 51.0% after removing one poorly-reported document). Data re-analysis studies had higher reproducibility (88.6%). Using p<0.05 threshold, 70.9% (82/116) of studies with extractable p-values were statistically significant.
evaluation: Claims C68-C81 present the main reproducibility findings. The data are clearly reported with appropriate caveats. The authors acknowledge that 38 studies (21.5%, mostly from one document) could not be assessed due to poor reporting, which is a significant limitation but transparently reported. The variation across disciplines is substantial, though sample sizes are small for some disciplines (e.g., economics N=5, education N=5), limiting confidence in cross-disciplinary comparisons.

result: The review identified 47 documents with 177 reproducibility studies from 2018-2019, predominantly in psychology and health sciences (>72%). The findings suggest possible unique disciplinary cultures around reproducibility, though some disciplines embed replication within original studies. Overall, only a small fraction of research in any discipline focuses on reproducing previously published work.
evaluation: Claims C82-C86 summarize key findings and offer interpretations. The data support the descriptive claims (C82-C83). The inference about disciplinary cultures (C84) is appropriately hedged with acknowledgment of limitations. The claim about embedded replications (C85) is based on field knowledge and is reasonable. The conclusion about the rarity of reproducibility studies (C86) is supported by the data and consistent with cited prior work.

result: A cited study found 10% of biomedical papers included reproducibility components, though most wouldn't qualify as independent replication studies by this review's criteria. Papers reporting multiple studies were more likely to report funding (81.8%) than single-study papers (63.9%), suggesting funders recognize reproducibility value and USA-based researchers lead in this area.
evaluation: Claims C87-C88 appropriately cite and interpret prior work (Serghiou et al., 2021). Claims C89-C91 draw reasonable inferences from the funding and geographic data, though these are speculative interpretations appropriately hedged with 'may suggest.' The data support the descriptive claim (C89), while C90-C91 are plausible but not definitively proven interpretations.

result: Only 11 of 47 papers reported reproducing multiple original studies, suggesting most reproducibility studies focus on single previous studies. Two 'single studies' were part of larger projects, and four reported multiple reproductions of the same original article.
evaluation: Claims C92-C95 describe the distribution of single vs. multiple reproducibility efforts. The data are clearly reported (C92, C94, C95), and the inference (C93) follows logically. The authors appropriately note nuances in how 'single study' was defined, enhancing transparency.

result: Only a minority of studies referred to registered protocols, with psychology having the highest rate (45.8%). Registered protocols enhance transparency and reduce bias, which seems especially relevant for reproducibility projects, though registration mandates are rare and discipline-specific.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 present data findings. Claims C98-C99 about protocol benefits are supported by citations (Nosek et al., 2018, 2019). Claims C100-C101 offer reasonable interpretations and acknowledge current practice limitations. The argument for protocol registration in reproducibility studies is logical and well-supported.

result: Study designs varied by discipline: psychology featured observational and experimental studies, while health sciences and economics emphasized data re-analysis. Reproducing observational/experimental studies may require more resources than data re-analysis, potentially explaining higher reproducibility rates for the latter. Publishing re-analyses showing identical results may be difficult in environments favoring novelty.
evaluation: Claims C102-C103 present data findings. Claim C104 offers a reasonable speculation about resource requirements explaining differential reproducibility rates, appropriately hedged with 'may.' Claim C105 is supported by citations (Ebrahim et al., 2014; Naudet et al., 2018) and represents a plausible publication bias concern.

result: Most reproducibility teams (66.1%) had no overlap or contact with original study authors. This finding may not generalize to disciplines embedding replication within original publications. Nosek and Errington advocate for discussing replication definitions before conducting studies, a practice not typically implemented despite potential benefits. However, original author involvement may increase allegiance bias, and many original authors don't respond to contact attempts.
evaluation: Claim C106 presents data findings. Claim C107 appropriately notes scope limitations. Claims C108-C109 accurately cite Nosek and Errington (2020b). Claim C110 draws a reasonable inference from the data. Claims C111-C112 present valid concerns about bias and non-response, with C112 supported by citations (Errington et al., 2021a,b; Kane and Kimmelman, 2021). The discussion balances benefits and risks of author involvement.

result: Psychology and health sciences studies tended to use effect size comparisons to define reproducibility success, though sample sizes in other disciplines were too small for meaningful comparison. There is increasing literature on different reproducibility definitions, and success rates unavoidably depend on how replication is defined.
evaluation: Claim C113 presents a data finding. Claim C114 appropriately acknowledges sample size limitations (economics N=5, education N=5, biomedicine N=6). Claims C115-C116 are well-supported by multiple citations (Errington et al., 2021a,b; Held et al., 2022; Pawel and Held, 2020) and represent an important conceptual point about definition-dependence of reproducibility rates.

result: This is claimed to be the first study providing broad cross-disciplinary comparison of explicit reproducibility study characteristics. The comparative approach may help identify features to support future reproducibility research.
evaluation: Claim C117 asserts novelty with 'to our knowledge,' which is difficult to verify without comprehensive literature review. The claim is plausible given the specific scope (explicit reproducibility studies across multiple disciplines in 2018-2019), but the hedging suggests appropriate uncertainty. Claim C118 is speculative about potential future value, appropriately hedged with 'may.'

result: The study has several acknowledged limitations: terminology may not have captured all studies; databases may not equally represent disciplines; only two years were examined, preventing temporal analysis and missing well-known studies; sample sizes in some disciplines were modest; only primary/first outcomes were extracted; reporting quality was sometimes poor; and screeners/extractors were not naïve to study aims.
evaluation: Claims C119-C128 transparently acknowledge multiple study limitations. These are reasonable concerns appropriately raised by the authors. The two-year restriction (C121-C123) was a pragmatic decision with clear trade-offs. The poor reporting quality (C127) is documented in the results (38 studies couldn't be assessed). The lack of blinding (C128) is a valid concern, though dual screening/extraction provides some quality control. The transparency in limitation reporting strengthens the overall credibility.

result: The explicit reproducibility studies targeted represent only part of the literature where reproducibility features may be embedded. Random samples show reproducibility concepts are not uncommon in biomedicine (Wallach et al., 2018), with 5% of psychology papers and 1% of social science papers being replications (Hardwicke et al., 2020). Some fields require replications within original publications, and meta-analyses suggest many topics have multiple similar studies. Different replication practices need further empirical study.
evaluation: Claim C129 appropriately acknowledges scope limitations. Claims C130-C132 accurately cite prior work showing varying rates of embedded reproducibility across fields. Claims C133-C134 make reasonable points about field practices and meta-analyses, with C134 supported by citation (Ioannidis, 2016). Claim C135 identifies an important research need. This contextualizes the study's findings within broader reproducibility landscape.

result: The finding that only about half of reproducibility studies reproduced is concerning but consistent with other studies. These estimates may not represent entire fields due to selection bias in which studies are chosen for replication. Reproducibility rates and definitions vary across fields, and definition choice may affect interpretation. This suggests need for disciplinary exchange on reproducibility approaches, methodological best practices, and multiple diverse studies with converging evidence. Explicit reproducibility studies are currently rare and need encouragement, incentivization, and support.
evaluation: Claims C136-C137 appropriately interpret the main finding with context from prior literature. Claim C138 raises a valid concern about selection bias that the authors cannot address with their data. Claims C139-C140 summarize key findings about definitional variation and its interpretive consequences. Claims C141-C145 offer reasonable recommendations based on the findings, appropriately hedged as suggestions rather than definitive prescriptions. The conclusions follow logically from the presented evidence while acknowledging limitations.

result: Reproducibility is a central tenet of research that helps discern discoveries from false leads, though the lexicon is poorly defined. Most studies are never formally reproduced, with some disciplines having lower rates than others. For example, only 0.13% of education research articles described reproducibility studies. There is rising concern about reproducibility and increasing interest in research transparency.
evaluation: Claims C1-C2 state foundational principles supported by general scientific knowledge. Claim C3 is supported by citation (Goodman et al., 2016). Claims C4-C5 represent established knowledge supported by subsequent examples. Claim C6 is supported by citation (Makel and Plucker, 2014) with specific data. Claims C7-C8 are supported by multiple citations indicating field-wide concern. These claims establish appropriate background context.

result: Prior large-scale reproducibility projects found concerning results: in psychology, only 36% of 100 studies had significant results (vs. 97% originally) and 47% had effect sizes within original 95% CIs. In economics, only 33% of 67 papers reproduced, with rates improving when original authors were involved. In cancer biology, most studies couldn't be attempted, most that were attempted didn't produce consistent results, and effects were only 15% of original. Non-reproducing medical studies may exaggerate patient benefits and harms.
evaluation: Claims C9-C10 accurately cite the Open Science Collaboration (2015) psychology reproducibility project. Claim C11 accurately cites Chang and Li (2015) economics study. Claims C12-C13 draw reasonable inferences from the economics findings. Claims C14-C16 accurately cite the cancer biology reproducibility project (Errington et al., 2021a,b; Kane and Kimmelman, 2021). Claim C17 is supported by citation (Le Noury et al., 2015). These claims establish the empirical basis for concern about reproducibility.

result: No data exists providing systematic reproducibility estimates across multiple disciplines or explaining why disciplines vary in reproducibility rates. Failure to empirically examine reproducibility contributes to research waste.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 identify a gap in the literature that motivates the current study. These claims are presented as knowledge statements about the state of the field at the time of writing. Claim C20 is supported by citations (Nasser et al., 2017; Ioannidis et al., 2014; Freedman et al., 2015). Together, these claims establish the rationale and significance of the current work.
